claims.statement: The Drinking Water Directive requires Member States to assess leakage levels and improvement potential, evidencing policy attention to measured leakage reduction.
The Data Act creates user access and third-party sharing rights for readily available connected-product data, subject to its scope and safeguards.

contrary_evidence: The directive's leakage assessment concerns water-supply infrastructure, not proof that apartment-building customers or insurers will buy indoor leak monitoring.

economics.acquisition_route: Bulk enrollment through property administrators, plumbing firms, and insurer-sponsored pilots rather than resident-by-resident sales
economics.founder_net_worth_path: Cover 10000 apartments by year 3 (unvalidated), 100000 apartments by year 7 (unvalidated), and support founder equity above PLN 5 million by year 8 (unvalidated)
economics.founder_time: 10-15 hours per week during validation (unvalidated), with plumbers installing devices
economics.gross_margin_basis: Reusable commodity sensors, automated triage, and plumber referral fees support 45-62% gross margin (unvalidated)
economics.payback: Hardware and channel cost recovered in 12-20 months (unvalidated)
economics.pricing: PLN 6-12 per apartment per month (unvalidated) plus 10-20% of documented avoided cost (unvalidated)
economics.retention_or_repeat: Three-year building subscriptions (unvalidated) and repeated incident-response referrals

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: Verified leak outcomes improve alert precision, property risk segmentation, and insurer evidence
fingerprint.customer: Housing cooperatives, administrators, insurers, and plumbing networks
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: Administrator portfolio contracts and plumber-installed kits
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: Sensor rental, alert triage, verified incident record, and shared-savings reporting
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: Administrator pays when a building activates monitoring; insurer may pay for a prevention cohort after approved results
fingerprint.problem_trigger: A leak claim, aging risers, insurer loss review, or repeated hidden-water damage

founder_fit: Quantified prevention aligns with founder interests.
Plumber and administrator channels minimize consumer selling.
Risk modeling and alert automation use data-science strengths.
risks: False alarms and missed leaks create reputational exposure.
The stated PLN 160000 startup capital requirement is unvalidated.

structure.commercial_archetype: Loss-prevention subscription and shared-savings risk pool
structure.control_point: Permissioned cross-building dataset linking sensor patterns, confirmed leaks, repair actions, and avoided-loss evidence
structure.critical_dependency: Administrators must permit installation and insurers or owners must recognize measurable savings from alerts

thesis: Deploy contract-authorized leak sensors through plumbers and housing administrators, combine alerts with verified incident and repair outcomes, and sell buildings a shared-savings monitoring service. With separate permission, pool anonymized building-level loss evidence for insurer prevention programs; the moat is the incident-linked dataset and administrator channel, not the commodity sensor.
title: LeakPool Housing Risk Network
uncertainties: Which sensor locations maximize verified loss prevention?
Can insurer funding materially lower administrator acquisition cost?
